prompt: A 70-kg 34-year-old man with known epilepsy is brought in with continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity that has now persisted for 10 minutes without recovery of consciousness. IV access is established. Airway is patent with the patient on oxygen, fingerstick glucose 96 mg/dL, temperature normal. He has not responded to a single pre-hospital dose of intranasal midazolam. Outline the stepwise pharmacologic management of convulsive status epilepticus including specific agents and doses for the emergent and urgent-control phases.
response_a:
This is convulsive status epilepticus and requires immediate, adequately dosed benzodiazepine therapy; underdosing benzodiazepines is one of the most common and consequential errors. Because IV access is present, the first-line agent is IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, which for this 70-kg patient is roughly 4 mg (typical single dose 4 mg, may repeat once after 5-10 minutes; do not exceed a total of about 8 mg). If IV lorazepam were unavailable, IM midazolam 10 mg or IV diazepam 0.15-0.2 mg/kg would be alternatives.

If seizures continue after adequate benzodiazepine dosing, move promptly to a second-line (urgent-control) IV antiseizure medication. Reasonable choices with good evidence (ESETT) include fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (up to 4.5 g), or valproate 40 mg/kg. These are considered roughly equivalent in efficacy, so selection depends on comorbidities: avoid valproate in hepatic disease or possible pregnancy, and use caution with fosphenytoin in cardiac conduction disease given the need for cardiac monitoring during infusion.

If status persists after a benzodiazepine plus a full second-line agent, this is refractory status epilepticus, and the patient should be intubated and started on a continuous anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital) with continuous EEG monitoring. Throughout, address the airway, check electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, and a toxicology and antiseizure-drug-level screen, and search for a precipitant such as missed medication, infection, or structural lesion.
response_b:
This is convulsive status epilepticus and the priority is rapid, correctly dosed benzodiazepine therapy. Since he already failed a single dose of intranasal midazolam and now has IV access, give IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, which is about 4 mg for this 70-kg man, and this can be repeated once after 5-10 minutes if seizures continue. Simultaneously secure the airway, provide oxygen, and confirm the glucose is adequate (it is, at 96).

If convulsions persist after benzodiazepines, proceed to a second-line IV antiseizure agent for urgent control. A widely used option is fosphenytoin at 10 mg PE/kg as a loading dose with cardiac monitoring; alternatives supported by the ESETT trial include levetiracetam 60 mg/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg, all considered comparably effective. Selection is guided by comorbidities, avoiding valproate in liver disease or pregnancy and using fosphenytoin cautiously in patients with cardiac conduction abnormalities.

If seizures continue despite a benzodiazepine and a full second-line agent, this is refractory status epilepticus requiring intubation and a continuous anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital) with continuous EEG. In parallel, send electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, antiseizure drug levels, and a toxicology screen, and pursue the underlying cause such as nonadherence, infection, metabolic derangement, or an acute structural lesion.

prompt: A 24-year-old woman is referred after two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. On careful history she reports several years of early-morning myoclonic jerks (dropping her coffee mug) and occasional brief absences; EEG shows 4-6 Hz generalized polyspike-and-wave, and MRI is normal. She is diagnosed with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. She is not currently trying to conceive but is sexually active and does not want to become pregnant right now; she uses a combined oral contraceptive. Recommend an antiseizure medication strategy and explain the key pitfalls in drug selection for this specific syndrome and patient.
response_a:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is a genetic generalized epilepsy that is usually lifelong and typically responds well to broad-spectrum antiseizure medications, but drug choice matters greatly here. In a young woman of childbearing potential, valproate should be avoided as first-line despite its high efficacy because of its major teratogenic risk (neural tube defects and dose-dependent reduction in childhood IQ and autism risk). My first choice would be levetiracetam, which has good efficacy against the generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures of JME and a relatively favorable reproductive-safety profile; lamotrigine is an alternative but must be used cautiously because it can aggravate myoclonic seizures in a subset of JME patients.

A critical and frequently missed interaction concerns lamotrigine and combined oral contraceptives: the estrogen component induces lamotrigine glucuronidation and can lower lamotrigine levels by roughly 50 percent, with rebound rises during the pill-free week, so lamotrigine dosing must be adjusted and this instability is another reason to favor levetiracetam here. I would also counsel her that narrow-spectrum sodium-channel agents such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, and gabapentin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures and should be avoided in JME.

Because she is a woman of reproductive age on an antiseizure medication, I would start high-dose folic acid (typically 4-5 mg daily) now, well before any potential conception, given that JME frequently requires lifelong therapy and pregnancies are often unplanned. I would also emphasize adherence, sleep hygiene, and avoidance of sleep deprivation and excess alcohol, which are common seizure triggers in this syndrome, and arrange follow-up to confirm seizure freedom and reassess the contraceptive/AED interaction.
response_b:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is a genetic generalized epilepsy that is generally lifelong and responds to broad-spectrum agents, and drug selection in this patient must account for her reproductive potential. Valproate, while historically the most effective drug for JME, should be avoided first-line in a woman who could become pregnant because of neural tube defects and dose-dependent neurodevelopmental harm. For this patient I would recommend lamotrigine as the drug of choice: it is broadly effective across the seizure types of JME, is generally well tolerated, and has one of the better reproductive-safety records among antiseizure medications, which makes it attractive for a young woman.

An important interaction to manage is between lamotrigine and her combined oral contraceptive: the estrogen induces lamotrigine metabolism and lowers its concentration substantially, with rebound during the hormone-free interval, so the lamotrigine dose typically needs to be increased and monitored, and any change in contraception should prompt reassessment. I would also warn against narrow-spectrum sodium-channel drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and phenytoin, which can paradoxically worsen the absence and myoclonic seizures characteristic of JME.

Because she is a woman of reproductive age on an antiseizure medication, I would begin high-dose folic acid (about 4-5 mg daily) now rather than waiting, given that JME usually requires long-term treatment and unplanned pregnancy is common. Finally, I would counsel her strongly on lifestyle triggers, sleep deprivation, alcohol, and photic stimulation, all of which are classic precipitants in JME, and arrange follow-up to confirm control and adjust therapy.

prompt: A 52-year-old woman with episodic migraine with aura (2-3 attacks/month, each disabling for 12-24 hours) asks for a better acute treatment; over-the-counter ibuprofen is no longer reliably effective. PMH: myocardial infarction 3 years ago with a drug-eluting stent, hypertension (well controlled on lisinopril and metoprolol), hyperlipidemia. No hemiplegic or brainstem-aura features. She is on aspirin 81 mg, clopidogrel was stopped last year, plus atorvastatin. Recommend an acute (abortive) migraine strategy for this patient and justify your drug choices given her history.
response_a:
The dominant consideration in this patient is her established coronary artery disease with a prior MI and stent, which fundamentally shapes acute migraine therapy. Triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) cause coronary vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in patients with ischemic heart disease, prior MI, uncontrolled hypertension, and in hemiplegic or brainstem (basilar) aura; ergotamine and dihydroergotamine are likewise contraindicated. So the mainstays of triptan and ergot therapy are off the table for her.

I would instead build her acute plan around agents without arterial vasoconstriction. First, optimize non-vasoconstrictive analgesia: a prescription NSAID such as naproxen or diclofenac if tolerated (weighing GI/renal risk on top of aspirin), combined with an antiemetic like metoclopramide or prochlorperazine that also has intrinsic anti-migraine efficacy. The newer options are especially attractive here: the gepants (ubrogepant or rimegepant, small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonists) have no vasoconstrictor effect and are considered safe in cardiovascular disease, and lasmiditan (a 5-HT1F agonist) also lacks vasoconstriction, though it causes dizziness/sedation and a driving restriction.

Given her attack frequency and disability, I would also discuss preventive therapy, since 2-3 disabling attacks monthly meets the threshold. Her metoprolol already offers some migraine prophylaxis; candesartan or a CGRP monoclonal antibody would be reasonable cardiac-safe additions. I would counsel her to limit acute treatment days to fewer than about 10 per month to avoid medication-overuse headache, and to control vascular risk factors aggressively.
response_b:
This patient has moderately frequent, disabling migraine with aura and needs a more effective abortive strategy than OTC ibuprofen, and the challenge is layering that onto significant coronary disease. A reasonable escalation is to a triptan, which remains the most effective migraine-specific abortive class; I would start sumatriptan 50-100 mg orally at onset, or a subcutaneous formulation for rapid, severe attacks, and pair it with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide to improve absorption and treat nausea. Because she has migraine with aura, she should take it early in the headache phase.

That said, her cardiovascular history warrants caution and monitoring: I would keep the triptan dose at the lower end, limit frequency, ensure her blood pressure stays controlled on her current lisinopril and metoprolol, and counsel her to report any chest tightness. If triptans are not tolerated, non-vasoconstrictive alternatives include the gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant) and lasmiditan, a 5-HT1F agonist without vasoconstriction, and a prescription NSAID such as naproxen can serve as adjunct or backup.

Given 2-3 disabling attacks per month, preventive therapy is also warranted. Her metoprolol already provides some prophylactic benefit, and candesartan or a CGRP monoclonal antibody would be reasonable additions. I would counsel her to keep acute-treatment days under roughly 10 per month to avoid medication-overuse headache and to remain aggressive about vascular risk-factor control, including her statin and antiplatelet therapy.

prompt: A 41-year-old man is brought to the ED with agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and fever (39.2 C). Vitals: HR 128, BP 158/96. He is confused. Two clinical scenarios are on the table and you must distinguish them: (1) he was recently started on a second serotonergic agent, versus (2) he was recently started on a high-potency antipsychotic. Compare serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in terms of causative agents, time course, key neuromuscular examination findings, and specific pharmacologic treatment, and explain how the exam would let you tell them apart.
response_a:
Both serotonin syndrome (SS) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) present with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status, but their pathophysiology, tempo, and exam findings differ. SS results from excess serotonergic activity (SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, and combinations) and characteristically develops rapidly, within 24 hours of a dose increase or a new agent. NMS results from central dopamine blockade (high-potency neuroleptics such as haloperidol, or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson disease) and evolves more insidiously over days.

The neuromuscular exam is the most useful discriminator. Serotonin syndrome classically produces hyporeflexia with generalized lead-pipe rigidity that is symmetric and diffuse, developing over one to three days; pupils are typically normal. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, by contrast, produces neuromuscular hyperexcitability, hyperreflexia, and spontaneous or inducible clonus that is most pronounced in the lower extremities, along with mydriasis, tremor, and hyperactive bowel sounds, and it comes on abruptly. Recognizing these opposite motor patterns is what lets you separate the two at the bedside.

Management differs accordingly. For serotonin syndrome, stop all serotonergic agents, give aggressive supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, cool the patient, and use dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg as the specific antidote for the muscular hyperactivity, with bromocriptine as an adjunct. For NMS, stop the offending drug and give cyproheptadine, a serotonin antagonist, 12 mg initially then 2 mg every 2 hours as needed. In severe cases of either syndrome with extreme hyperthermia, intubation, paralysis, and active cooling are warranted, and CK, renal function, and coagulation should be monitored for rhabdomyolysis and DIC.
response_b:
Both serotonin syndrome (SS) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) share hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status, but they differ in cause, tempo, and, most usefully, the neuromuscular exam. SS arises from excess serotonergic activity (SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans, and their combinations) and typically develops rapidly, within 24 hours of starting or increasing a serotonergic drug. NMS results from central dopamine-receptor blockade (high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol) or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy, and it evolves more slowly over one to three days.

The motor exam is the key discriminator. Serotonin syndrome produces neuromuscular hyperactivity: hyperreflexia and spontaneous or inducible clonus, characteristically greater in the lower extremities, along with tremor, mydriasis, and hyperactive bowel sounds, developing quickly. NMS instead produces diffuse lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia (bradyreflexia) and a bradykinetic, extrapyramidal picture that comes on gradually. So clonus and hyperreflexia point toward serotonin syndrome, whereas lead-pipe rigidity with depressed reflexes points toward NMS.

Treatment follows the mechanism. For serotonin syndrome: stop all serotonergic drugs, provide supportive care and benzodiazepines, cool aggressively, and use cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist), typically 12 mg initially then 2 mg every 2 hours as needed, as the specific antidote. For NMS: stop the causative antipsychotic and use dantrolene for the muscular rigidity and hyperthermia, with bromocriptine or amantadine to restore dopaminergic tone. In severe cases of either, intubation with neuromuscular blockade and active cooling may be needed, and CK, renal function, and coagulation should be followed for rhabdomyolysis and its complications.

prompt: A 58-year-old woman with severe treatment-resistant major depressive disorder has failed adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, and bupropion-augmentation. Her psychiatrist wants to switch her to the MAOI phenelzine. She is currently taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily (switched to it 3 weeks ago from her prior regimen) plus trazodone 50 mg at night for sleep. She has no significant medical comorbidities. Describe exactly how you would transition her onto phenelzine safely, including washout requirements, and outline the counseling she needs for ongoing MAOI therapy.
response_a:
The transition from a serotonergic antidepressant to an MAOI is one of the highest-risk switches in psychiatry because overlap can precipitate life-threatening serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis, so an adequate washout is non-negotiable. The critical point here is fluoxetine's very long half-life: fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine persist for weeks, so a washout of at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine is required before phenelzine can be started. This is much longer than the standard 2-week washout that applies to shorter-acting SSRIs/SNRIs. Her trazodone (also serotonergic) should be stopped and washed out as well; a shorter interval is acceptable for trazodone given its short half-life, but it must not overlap with the MAOI.

Operationally, I would stop fluoxetine now, provide a non-serotonergic bridge for sleep or symptoms if needed (avoiding any serotonergic hypnotic), and wait the full 5 weeks before initiating phenelzine, titrating from 15 mg. When later stopping phenelzine to switch to another antidepressant, a 2-week MAOI washout is required before starting a serotonergic drug, to allow regeneration of monoamine oxidase.

Counseling for ongoing MAOI therapy is extensive: she must follow a tyramine-restricted diet (avoiding aged cheeses, cured/fermented meats, tap/draft beer, soy, sauerkraut, and other fermented foods) to prevent hypertensive crisis, and she must avoid sympathomimetics (decongestants like pseudoephedrine), meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, other serotonergic antidepressants, and triptans. She should recognize the warning signs of hypertensive crisis (severe occipital headache, palpitations, chest pain) and of serotonin syndrome, and she must inform all providers and pharmacists that she is on an MAOI before any new medication is added.
response_b:
Switching from a serotonergic antidepressant to an MAOI such as phenelzine carries a high risk of serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crisis, so the washout is the crux of doing this safely. I would stop both fluoxetine and the trazodone now, since both are serotonergic and must be fully cleared before starting the MAOI. Trazodone has a short half-life and clears quickly, so its washout is not the limiting factor here.

For the washout duration, the standard rule is a 2-week drug-free interval between stopping an SSRI/SNRI and starting an MAOI, which allows the serotonin system to reset, and I would apply that 2-week washout after stopping her fluoxetine before initiating phenelzine, titrating from 15 mg upward as tolerated. In the reverse direction, when discontinuing phenelzine to move to another antidepressant, a 2-week MAOI washout is likewise required to allow regeneration of monoamine oxidase before a serotonergic drug is introduced.

Counseling for maintenance MAOI therapy is substantial. She must adhere to a tyramine-restricted diet, avoiding aged cheeses, cured and fermented meats, draft beer, soy products, and sauerkraut to prevent tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis. She must also avoid sympathomimetic decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, as well as meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, triptans, and other serotonergic antidepressants. I would teach her to recognize the symptoms of a hypertensive crisis (severe pounding headache, palpitations, chest pain) and serotonin syndrome, and to notify every clinician and pharmacist that she takes an MAOI before starting any new medication.

prompt: A 46-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium (last level 0.8 mEq/L, stable for years) presents with a 4-day history of coarse tremor, nausea, vomiting, mild confusion, and unsteady gait. Two weeks ago her primary care doctor started hydrochlorothiazide for newly diagnosed hypertension, and she has also been taking ibuprofen several times daily for back pain. She reports poor oral intake and reduced urine output over the past 2 days. Explain the likely mechanism, the drug interactions involved, what you would check, and how lithium should be monitored and managed long-term.
response_a:
This picture, coarse tremor, GI upset, ataxia, and confusion in a chronically stable lithium patient, is classic for lithium toxicity precipitated by recent medication changes and volume depletion. Lithium is handled almost entirely by the kidney and is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule in parallel with sodium. Anything that reduces renal lithium clearance will raise levels. Both of her new exposures do exactly that: thiazide diuretics cause volume contraction and increase proximal sodium (and therefore lithium) reabsorption, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce renal prostaglandins and glomerular filtration, both of which decrease lithium excretion and raise serum lithium. Her poor intake and reduced urine output compound this by adding dehydration and prerenal azotemia.

I would immediately check a serum lithium level, basic metabolic panel (sodium, creatinine/eGFR, and volume status), and an ECG. Management is to stop the lithium, hydrochlorothiazide, and ibuprofen, and to restore volume with isotropic saline, which enhances lithium excretion; hemodialysis is indicated for severe toxicity (typically levels above roughly 4 mEq/L, or above 2.5 with significant symptoms or renal impairment, or when the patient cannot clear it). The therapeutic range to target on maintenance is generally 0.6-1.0 mEq/L (up to about 1.2 in acute mania).

Long-term, lithium requires structured monitoring: periodic levels (every 6-12 months when stable, and after any dose change or interacting-drug change), along with renal function, thyroid function (TSH), and calcium, since lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism. I would counsel her to maintain steady salt and fluid intake, to avoid NSAIDs (using acetaminophen instead), and to coordinate with psychiatry whenever any new medication, especially a diuretic, ACE inhibitor/ARB, or NSAID, is started, since all of these can raise lithium levels.
response_b:
Her presentation, coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia, and confusion in a previously stable lithium patient, strongly suggests altered lithium handling after two new medications and volume depletion. Lithium is cleared renally in parallel with sodium, so its concentration is very sensitive to renal blood flow, GFR, and sodium balance. The key point about her two new drugs is their effect on lithium clearance: thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide promote natriuresis and, by increasing renal sodium and lithium elimination, tend to increase lithium excretion, while NSAIDs similarly enhance renal clearance; the main concern with these combinations is therefore a risk of subtherapeutic lithium and loss of mood stabilization rather than accumulation. Her dehydration and low urine output, however, will independently concentrate the drug and are likely the dominant driver of her symptoms here.

I would immediately obtain a serum lithium level, a basic metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR and sodium, an assessment of volume status, and an ECG. Management is to hold lithium, hydrochlorothiazide, and ibuprofen, rehydrate with isotonic saline to promote clearance, and consider hemodialysis for severe toxicity (levels above roughly 4 mEq/L, or above 2.5 with serious symptoms or renal impairment). The maintenance therapeutic range is generally 0.6-1.0 mEq/L, up to about 1.2 mEq/L in acute mania.

Long-term, lithium demands structured monitoring: periodic serum levels (every 6-12 months when stable and after any dose or interacting-drug change), plus renal function, TSH, and calcium, because lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism. I would counsel her to keep salt and fluid intake steady, prefer acetaminophen over NSAIDs, and always coordinate with psychiatry before starting new medications such as diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, or NSAIDs, since these can meaningfully change lithium levels.

prompt: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson disease (Hoehn-Yahr stage 3) on carbidopa-levodopa and pramipexole has two new problems. First, he has developed significant nausea, partly attributed to his dopaminergic medications, and the ED physician who saw him last week for a fall gave him a medication for nausea after which his rigidity and bradykinesia acutely worsened. Second, over the past month he has developed visual hallucinations (seeing children in the house) with preserved insight but rising distress. Address (a) appropriate antiemetic selection in Parkinson disease and (b) the evaluation and pharmacologic management of Parkinson disease psychosis.
response_a:
Antiemetic selection in Parkinson disease is a common and dangerous pitfall because most standard antiemetics are central dopamine-receptor antagonists that cross the blood-brain barrier and acutely worsen parkinsonism, which is almost certainly what happened after his ED visit. For nausea in PD, the appropriate first choices are agents that do not block central dopamine: ondansetron (a 5-HT3 antagonist) or domperidone (a peripheral dopamine antagonist that largely spares the CNS). Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine must be avoided because they penetrate the CNS and block striatal D2 receptors, worsening motor symptoms and potentially precipitating a parkinsonian crisis. I would also review whether the nausea can be reduced by taking levodopa with food or adjusting the dopamine agonist.

For the hallucinations, the first step is evaluation, not immediately reaching for an antipsychotic. Parkinson disease psychosis is often provoked or worsened by an intercurrent problem (infection, especially UTI, metabolic derangement, dehydration) or by the medications themselves. I would screen for delirium and infection and then simplify the dopaminergic regimen in order of the drugs most likely to cause psychosis and least likely to help motor function: taper/stop anticholinergics first, then amantadine, then MAO-B inhibitors and dopamine agonists (his pramipexole is a prime suspect), reducing levodopa last since it does the heavy lifting for mobility.

If hallucinations remain distressing despite these steps, add a pharmacologic agent that treats psychosis without blocking dopamine and worsening motor function. Pimavanserin (a selective 5-HT2A inverse agonist) is specifically approved for PD psychosis; quetiapine is a commonly used low-potency alternative; and clozapine has the strongest evidence but requires ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis. Typical antipsychotics (haloperidol) and most atypicals with strong D2 blockade (risperidone, olanzapine) must be avoided because they markedly worsen parkinsonism.
response_b:
Antiemetic selection is a critical issue in Parkinson disease because the most common cause of acute motor worsening from an antiemetic is central dopamine blockade. For this patient's nausea, I would first try measures such as taking levodopa with a small snack and reassessing the dopamine agonist. If a drug is needed, prochlorperazine or metoclopramide are effective and reasonable choices for dopaminergic nausea and can be used at low doses with monitoring, and ondansetron is an additional option. The goal is to control nausea so he maintains his antiparkinsonian regimen and nutrition.

For the hallucinations, evaluation comes before pharmacologic treatment. Parkinson disease psychosis is frequently triggered by an intercurrent illness (particularly urinary tract infection), metabolic disturbance, or dehydration, or by the antiparkinsonian drugs themselves. I would screen for delirium and infection, then rationalize the medication regimen from the agents most likely to provoke psychosis and least essential for motor control: stop anticholinergics first, then amantadine, then MAO-B inhibitors and dopamine agonists such as his pramipexole, and reduce levodopa last because it is most important for mobility.

If distressing hallucinations persist despite these measures, add an agent that does not aggravate parkinsonism. Pimavanserin, a selective 5-HT2A inverse agonist, is specifically approved for Parkinson disease psychosis; quetiapine is a widely used low-potency alternative; and clozapine has the best evidence but mandates neutrophil monitoring for agranulocytosis. High-potency typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol and higher-D2-affinity atypicals such as risperidone and olanzapine should be avoided because they substantially worsen motor function.

prompt: A 29-year-old woman presents with 4 days of progressive painful vision loss in the right eye, worse with eye movement, and a relative afferent pupillary defect on that side; visual acuity is 20/80. Brain MRI shows several periventricular and juxtacortical T2 hyperintensities, some ovoid and perpendicular to the ventricles, and an enhancing right optic nerve lesion; a couple of the brain lesions enhance and several do not. CSF shows oligoclonal bands. She is otherwise healthy. Discuss the diagnosis, the evidence-based acute management of this presentation, and what to avoid.
response_a:
This is an acute demyelinating optic neuritis, and the overall picture, a young woman with optic neuritis plus multiple periventricular/juxtacortical ovoid lesions (some enhancing, some not, indicating dissemination in time) and CSF oligoclonal bands, is highly consistent with multiple sclerosis by the McDonald criteria. The simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions satisfies dissemination in time, and the lesion distribution satisfies dissemination in space, so she likely already meets diagnostic criteria for MS.

For acute management of the optic neuritis/relapse, the evidence-based treatment is high-dose corticosteroids: intravenous methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3-5 days (an oral bioequivalent high-dose regimen is an acceptable alternative). Steroids speed the recovery of the acute attack but do not change the ultimate degree of visual recovery or long-term disability. The key lesson from the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial is what to avoid: low-dose oral prednisone (e.g., 1 mg/kg/day) used as monotherapy is contraindicated because it provided no benefit and was associated with an increased rate of recurrent optic neuritis. For patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to steroids and have severe visual loss, plasma exchange is a second-line option.

Beyond the acute attack, because she likely meets criteria for relapsing MS, she should be referred promptly to initiate a disease-modifying therapy to reduce future relapses and disability accrual; the specific agent (from platform injectables to high-efficacy monoclonal antibodies) is chosen based on disease activity and patient factors. I would also check vitamin D, counsel on smoking cessation, and screen for infection before steroids, while providing gastroprotection and monitoring glucose during the steroid course.
response_b:
This is an acute demyelinating optic neuritis. Combined with her MRI (multiple periventricular and juxtacortical ovoid lesions, some enhancing and some not) and CSF oligoclonal bands, the presentation is strongly consistent with multiple sclerosis under the McDonald criteria: dissemination in space is met by the lesion distribution, and the coexistence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions supports dissemination in time, so she likely already fulfills diagnostic criteria for MS.

For acute treatment of the optic neuritis, corticosteroids are the mainstay, and I would use oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day with a taper as first-line therapy, reserving intravenous methylprednisolone for patients who fail to improve or who have particularly severe deficits. Steroids hasten recovery of the acute episode but do not alter the final level of vision or long-term disability. If there is severe, steroid-refractory visual loss, plasma exchange is a reasonable escalation. Before starting steroids I would screen for infection, provide gastroprotection, and monitor glucose.

Beyond the attack, since she likely meets criteria for relapsing MS, she should be referred promptly to begin a disease-modifying therapy to reduce future relapse rate and disability, with the specific agent chosen according to disease activity and patient preference across the spectrum from platform injectables to higher-efficacy monoclonal antibodies. I would also check vitamin D and strongly counsel smoking cessation, both of which influence long-term MS outcomes.

prompt: An 82-year-old woman is postoperative day 2 after repair of a hip fracture. Overnight she became agitated, pulling at lines, disoriented, and hypervigilant, with waxing-and-waning attention; her daughter says she was cognitively sharp at baseline. Medications include oxycodone PRN, a scopolamine patch for nausea, diphenhydramine for sleep, and cefazolin. Vitals: T 37.9, HR 104, BP 150/88, SpO2 92% on room air. Describe your workup for this presentation and your approach to management, including pharmacologic principles for agitation.
