She has no planned procedures. What are the appropriate RBC and platelet transfusion thresholds and your rationale?
response_a:
In a stable hospitalized patient without active bleeding or acute coronary syndrome, a restrictive RBC transfusion strategy is supported by high-quality evidence and endorsed by AABB guidelines. For a patient who is hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic, transfusing to keep the hemoglobin above 9 g/dL is a reasonable target in an actively myelosuppressed oncology patient, because maintaining a higher hemoglobin improves tolerance of ongoing cytopenias and reduces fatigue during count recovery. I would therefore transfuse red cells now with a goal hemoglobin of 9-10 g/dL and reassess.

For platelets, the prophylactic transfusion threshold in a stable, afebrile patient without bleeding is 10,000/uL. Her platelet count of 11,000 is essentially at that threshold, so I would recheck and transfuse one unit of apheresis platelets if she drops to or below 10,000, or sooner if fever, bleeding, or a procedure intervenes. Higher thresholds apply in specific settings: 20,000 with fever or sepsis, 50,000 for invasive procedures or active bleeding, and 100,000 for CNS bleeding or neurosurgery.

I would monitor daily counts, examine for occult bleeding, avoid unnecessary venipunctures and antiplatelet agents, and continue supportive care through the neutropenic nadir. Iron studies and hemolysis labs are generally unnecessary here, as the anemia is expected marrow suppression.
response_b:
In a stable hospitalized patient without active bleeding, symptoms, or acute coronary syndrome, a restrictive RBC transfusion strategy is supported by high-quality randomized data (TRICC and subsequent trials) and AABB guidelines. The evidence supports a transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL for stable inpatients, including stable oncology and critically ill patients, with a threshold of 8 g/dL reserved for those with preexisting cardiovascular disease or undergoing cardiac/orthopedic surgery. Because she is asymptomatic, stable, and without cardiac disease at a hemoglobin of 7.3, I would not transfuse red cells now and would recheck; single-unit transfusion with reassessment is the correct approach if she becomes symptomatic or drops below 7.

For platelets, the prophylactic transfusion threshold in a stable, afebrile patient without bleeding is 10,000/uL. Her count of 11,000 is just above threshold, so I would recheck and transfuse one unit of apheresis platelets if she reaches or falls below 10,000, or earlier if fever, bleeding, or a planned procedure supervenes. Higher thresholds apply in defined settings: 20,000 with fever or sepsis, 50,000 for invasive procedures or active bleeding, and 100,000 for CNS bleeding or neurosurgery.

I would monitor daily counts, examine for occult bleeding, minimize unnecessary phlebotomy and avoid antiplatelet agents, and continue supportive care through the neutropenic nadir. Iron studies and hemolysis workup are generally unnecessary here, as the anemia reflects expected chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression.

prompt: A 59-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and Gram-negative sepsis develops diffuse oozing from IV sites, hematuria, and ecchymoses. Labs: platelets 42,000, PT 21 s (elevated), aPTT 48 s (elevated), fibrinogen 95 mg/dL, D-dimer markedly elevated, schistocytes present. He is not currently on anticoagulation. He is bleeding but not hemodynamically unstable. Outline your management of this coagulopathy.
response_a:
This is acute, bleeding-predominant DIC secondary to Gram-negative sepsis. The single most important intervention is aggressive treatment of the underlying trigger, meaning source control and appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics for his sepsis; the coagulopathy will not resolve until the driver is controlled. Supportive blood-product replacement is guided by the degree of bleeding and the specific deficits rather than by lab numbers alone.

Because he is actively bleeding, I would transfuse platelets to keep the count above 50,000, give fresh frozen plasma to correct the prolonged PT/aPTT and replace consumed factors, and give cryoprecipitate to raise fibrinogen above 100-150 mg/dL given his hypofibrinogenemia. Antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid are generally contraindicated in DIC because inhibiting fibrinolysis in the setting of widespread microthrombosis can precipitate catastrophic organ-threatening thrombosis; the notable exception is the hyperfibrinolytic DIC of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Therapeutic heparin is reserved for thrombosis-predominant DIC, not this bleeding phenotype.

I would follow serial platelets, PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, and D-dimer every 6-12 hours to track response, continue targeted product support, and prioritize resolution of the sepsis. Vitamin K and folate repletion are reasonable adjuncts, and I would avoid unnecessary invasive procedures while he is coagulopathic.
response_b:
This is acute, bleeding-predominant DIC triggered by Gram-negative sepsis. The cornerstone of management is aggressive treatment of the underlying cause: source control and appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics, since the consumptive coagulopathy will persist until the septic driver is addressed. Blood-product support is tailored to the bleeding and to the specific hemostatic deficits rather than to laboratory values in isolation.

Because he is actively bleeding, I would transfuse platelets targeting a count above 50,000, administer fresh frozen plasma to correct the prolonged PT/aPTT and replace consumed coagulation factors, and give cryoprecipitate to raise fibrinogen above 100-150 mg/dL given the marked hypofibrinogenemia. I would also start tranexamic acid to reduce the diffuse mucosal and IV-site bleeding, as controlling the fibrinolytic component helps stabilize clot and limit transfusion requirements while source control is achieved. Therapeutic heparin, by contrast, is reserved for thrombosis-predominant DIC rather than this bleeding phenotype.

I would trend serial platelets, PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, and D-dimer every 6-12 hours to gauge response, continue targeted product replacement, and prioritize resolution of the sepsis. Vitamin K and folate repletion are reasonable adjuncts, and I would avoid unnecessary invasive procedures while he remains coagulopathic.

prompt: A 63-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and a biologic presents with fatigue. Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 79 fL, RDW 17%, ferritin 68 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 8%, CRP 42 mg/L (elevated), reticulocyte count low. She has no overt GI symptoms. How do you interpret these iron studies, and what is your diagnosis and management?
response_a:
The clinical challenge here is distinguishing anemia of chronic disease/inflammation from iron deficiency, and importantly recognizing that they frequently coexist in rheumatoid arthritis. The critical interpretive point is that ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and is falsely elevated by active inflammation, so a 'normal-range' ferritin does NOT exclude iron deficiency in an inflammatory state. In the setting of significant inflammation (elevated CRP), the ferritin cutoff for iron deficiency is raised to roughly 100 ng/mL, and a ferritin below 100 with a transferrin saturation of only 8% strongly supports true iron deficiency, likely superimposed on anemia of inflammation.

Her microcytosis (MCV 79), elevated RDW, very low transferrin saturation, and ferritin of 68 in the face of inflammation point to iron-deficient erythropoiesis. I would pursue a GI source (fecal occult blood, and given her age, colonoscopy/EGD) because occult GI blood loss must be excluded, and I would treat the iron deficiency. In active inflammation, oral iron absorption is impaired (hepcidin-mediated), so IV iron is often the more effective route. A soluble transferrin receptor level or sTfR/log-ferritin index can further confirm iron deficiency if diagnostic uncertainty remains.

I would also optimize control of her RA, since better inflammatory control lowers hepcidin and improves the anemia of inflammation component. Follow-up should include reassessment of hemoglobin and iron indices after repletion and treatment of any identified GI lesion.
response_b:
The clinical challenge is separating anemia of chronic disease/inflammation from iron deficiency in a patient with active rheumatoid arthritis, and the two commonly coexist. The iron studies must be read in the context of her inflammation. Her ferritin of 68 ng/mL is within the normal range, and since ferritin is the best single marker of body iron stores, a value in this range effectively rules out absolute iron deficiency. The picture is therefore most consistent with anemia of chronic inflammation: mild microcytosis, low reticulocytes, low transferrin saturation from hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration, and elevated CRP reflecting active disease.

The low transferrin saturation here reflects functional iron restriction driven by inflammation rather than true iron-store depletion, which is expected in anemia of chronic disease and does not by itself indicate a need for iron supplementation. I would focus on optimizing control of her rheumatoid arthritis, since reducing inflammation lowers hepcidin and improves iron availability and erythropoiesis. A soluble transferrin receptor level could be checked if there is residual uncertainty, but given the normal ferritin I would not empirically treat for iron deficiency.

I would reassess hemoglobin after intensifying RA control and monitor iron indices over time. If she later develops GI symptoms or the ferritin falls, a GI evaluation for occult blood loss would then be warranted. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are generally not first-line for anemia of inflammation of this severity.

prompt: A 44-year-old woman presents with fatigue, gingival bleeding, and easy bruising. CBC: WBC 3.2, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, platelets 22,000. Coagulation studies show PT and aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen 110 mg/dL, elevated D-dimer. Peripheral smear shows abnormal promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods. The hematopathologist calls to say the morphology strongly suggests acute promyelocytic leukemia; PML-RARA molecular confirmation is pending. What is your immediate management?
response_a:
Suspected APL is a medical emergency because of its associated life-threatening coagulopathy (a mixed DIC and hyperfibrinolysis), and early hemorrhagic death is the leading cause of induction mortality. The single most important action is to start all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) IMMEDIATELY on clinical/morphologic suspicion, without waiting for PML-RARA confirmation, because ATRA rapidly mitigates the coagulopathy and the risk of catastrophic bleeding accrues in the first hours to days.

Simultaneously, I would provide aggressive blood-product support: transfuse platelets to keep the count above 30,000-50,000, give cryoprecipitate to maintain fibrinogen above 150 mg/dL, and use fresh frozen plasma to correct coagulopathy, with frequent (every 6-12 hour) monitoring of CBC, fibrinogen, and coagulation studies. Confirmatory testing (PML-RARA by PCR/FISH, cytogenetics) should proceed in parallel, and definitive therapy typically pairs ATRA with arsenic trioxide (or anthracycline in high-risk disease). I would monitor closely for differentiation (APL) syndrome, treating with dexamethasone if it develops.

Supportive measures include avoiding invasive procedures, careful management of the coagulopathy around any necessary lines, and leukapheresis avoidance (it can worsen coagulopathy). This upfront, empiric approach to ATRA and product support is what has transformed APL into a highly curable leukemia.
response_b:
Suspected APL is a hematologic emergency, principally because of its severe coagulopathy combining DIC and hyperfibrinolysis, which drives early fatal hemorrhage. Management must be aggressive and immediate, centered on correcting the coagulopathy and confirming the diagnosis so that targeted therapy is applied appropriately.

I would provide intensive blood-product support right away: transfuse platelets to keep the count above 30,000-50,000, give cryoprecipitate to maintain fibrinogen above 150 mg/dL, and use fresh frozen plasma to correct the prolonged PT/aPTT, with frequent monitoring of CBC, fibrinogen, and coagulation parameters every 6-12 hours. Because ATRA carries its own risks, including differentiation syndrome and the potential for inappropriate exposure if the diagnosis is not APL, I would confirm the diagnosis with urgent PML-RARA testing (PCR/FISH) before committing to ATRA, and initiate it as soon as the molecular result returns. Definitive therapy then pairs ATRA with arsenic trioxide, with anthracycline added in high-risk disease.

Supportive care includes avoiding invasive procedures, meticulous coagulopathy management around any necessary central access, and avoiding leukapheresis, which can worsen the coagulopathy. I would monitor closely for differentiation syndrome once ATRA is started and treat it promptly with dexamethasone. This combination of prompt product support and diagnosis-directed ATRA reflects the modern, highly curable approach to APL.

prompt: A 77-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target INR 2-3) presents with a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage confirmed on CT. INR is 3.8. Weight 80 kg. Blood pressure 178/95, GCS 13, expanding hematoma concern. He last took warfarin this morning. What is your specific anticoagulation reversal strategy, including agents and doses?
response_a:
This is life-threatening, warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage, and rapid, complete reversal of the INR is the priority alongside blood pressure control and neurosurgical consultation. The mainstay of vitamin K antagonist reversal in major bleeding is intravenous vitamin K plus a rapid factor-replacement product. I would give vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV infusion immediately, which provides sustained correction by restoring hepatic synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X over the ensuing hours.

For immediate factor replacement, I would use fresh frozen plasma dosed at 15 mL/kg (approximately 1,200 mL for an 80 kg patient), which replaces the deficient vitamin K-dependent factors and corrects the coagulopathy while the vitamin K takes effect. I would recheck the INR after infusion and repeat plasma as needed to achieve and maintain an INR below 1.5. Concurrently, blood pressure should be lowered (systolic target around 140 mmHg), and neurosurgery should be involved urgently.

I would repeat coagulation studies frequently, watch for volume overload during plasma infusion, and hold all anticoagulation. Decisions about if and when to resume anticoagulation for his atrial fibrillation should be deferred and individualized, typically weeks later, weighing rebleeding risk against thromboembolic risk.
response_b:
This is life-threatening, warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage requiring immediate and complete INR reversal, together with blood pressure control and urgent neurosurgical involvement. The guideline-endorsed reversal for major/life-threatening VKA bleeding is four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) plus intravenous vitamin K, which achieves faster and more reliable INR correction than plasma and avoids the large volume load.

I would give 4F-PCC dosed by weight and INR: for an INR of 3.8 (in the 2 to <4 range), 25 units/kg (approximately 2,000 units for 80 kg, capped per protocol), administered immediately. I would give vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV infusion concurrently to sustain the correction, because PCC's effect is transient and factor levels can fall again without vitamin K. I would recheck the INR shortly after PCC to confirm correction below 1.5 and redose if necessary. Blood pressure should be lowered promptly (systolic target around 140 mmHg), and neurosurgery consulted urgently. Fresh frozen plasma would be a fallback only if PCC were unavailable.

I would repeat coagulation studies frequently, monitor for the small thrombotic risk of PCC, and hold all anticoagulation. Whether and when to resume anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation should be deferred and individualized, generally weeks later, balancing rebleeding against thromboembolic risk.

prompt: A 66-year-old woman presents with acute dyspnea; CT pulmonary angiogram shows bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. Blood pressure 118/74, HR 108, SpO2 93% on room air. Troponin is mildly elevated; BNP elevated; echocardiogram shows moderate RV dilation and hypokinesis. She has no active bleeding, normal renal function, and no recent surgery. sPESI is 1 (age). She remains normotensive and mentating well. What is the appropriate management, and is thrombolysis indicated?
response_a:
She has acute PE that is normotensive but with evidence of RV dysfunction (echo) and myocardial injury (troponin), placing her in the intermediate-high risk category. The pivotal management question is whether to give systemic thrombolysis, and the evidence, principally the PEITHO trial, is clear: routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive intermediate-risk PE reduces hemodynamic decompensation but at the cost of a significant excess of major bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage, with no overall mortality benefit. Therefore thrombolysis is NOT indicated up front in a stable, normotensive patient like this.

The correct management is prompt therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH or a DOAC) with close monitoring in a setting where escalation is possible, ideally a step-down or ICU bed for the first 24-72 hours. Systemic thrombolysis (or catheter-directed therapy/embolectomy) is held in reserve as rescue therapy should she develop hemodynamic deterioration (hypotension or shock). This 'watchful anticoagulation with rescue reperfusion' strategy is the standard of care for intermediate-high risk PE.

I would trend her hemodynamics, oxygenation, and cardiac biomarkers, ensure IV access and a plan for rapid escalation, and involve a PE response team if available. If she remains stable, she can transition to oral anticoagulation and step down, with a total anticoagulation course of at least 3 months and reassessment for provoking factors.
response_b:
She has acute PE that is normotensive but with both RV dysfunction on echocardiography and elevated troponin, which defines intermediate-high risk PE. Given the combination of imaging-confirmed RV strain and biomarker-confirmed myocardial injury together with her hypoxemia and tachycardia, systemic thrombolysis is indicated to relieve RV strain and prevent progression to hemodynamic collapse. I would administer alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours, provided she has no contraindications to fibrinolysis, followed by therapeutic anticoagulation once the coagulation parameters permit.

The rationale is that intermediate-high risk patients with demonstrable RV dysfunction are at meaningful risk of decompensation, and early reperfusion reduces that risk; withholding thrombolysis until frank shock develops exposes her to a high-mortality event. Catheter-directed thrombolysis would be a reasonable alternative if bleeding risk were a concern, but full-dose systemic thrombolysis is appropriate here given her normal renal function and absence of bleeding or recent surgery.

I would manage her in an ICU or step-down setting with continuous monitoring of hemodynamics, oxygenation, and cardiac biomarkers, and involve a PE response team if available. After thrombolysis and stabilization, she would transition to therapeutic anticoagulation with a DOAC or LMWH, continued for at least 3 months with reassessment for provoking factors and bleeding risk.

prompt: A 70-year-old man with relapsed CLL is to start venetoclax. He has bulky lymphadenopathy (largest node 6 cm), an absolute lymphocyte count of 85,000, and CrCl of 55 mL/min. He is assessed as high risk for tumor lysis syndrome. Describe the correct way to initiate venetoclax, including dosing schedule and TLS prophylaxis/monitoring.
response_a:
Venetoclax is a highly potent BCL-2 inhibitor that can cause rapid, massive tumor lysis, and fatal TLS occurred early in its development before a mandatory dose-ramp protocol was adopted. He is high risk for TLS given his bulky nodal disease (>5 cm) and high ALC, and this dictates both aggressive prophylaxis and inpatient monitoring. It is essential NOT to start at the target dose.

Because he is high risk, I would begin venetoclax with the standard 5-week ramp-up but with the first dose given at 20 mg in the inpatient setting, escalating weekly through 20, 50, 100, 200, and 400 mg only after confirming that laboratory parameters are stable at each step. This gradual escalation is the single most important measure to prevent catastrophic TLS. Given the high risk, I would start allopurinol 2-3 days before the first dose and ensure it is continued, and given his renal function and disease burden, I would also administer rasburicase and ensure aggressive IV and oral hydration.

Monitoring for a high-risk patient includes hospitalization for the 20 mg and 50 mg doses, with blood chemistries (potassium, phosphate, uric acid, calcium, creatinine) checked pre-dose, then at 6-8 hours and 24 hours after each escalation. I would correct electrolyte abnormalities promptly and involve nephrology if renal function or electrolytes deteriorate. Dose interruptions and slower re-escalation are used if TLS develops.
response_b:
Venetoclax is a potent BCL-2 inhibitor capable of producing rapid, life-threatening tumor lysis, and early fatal TLS events led to the mandatory dose-ramp-up schedule that must be followed. This patient is high risk for TLS given bulky lymphadenopathy (largest node >5 cm) and a high absolute lymphocyte count, which mandates the most intensive prophylaxis and monitoring.

Initiation must use the stepwise 5-week ramp-up: 20 mg daily for week 1, then 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, and finally 400 mg daily, advancing only once each step is tolerated and chemistries are stable; starting at the target dose is contraindicated. For a high-risk patient I would begin allopurinol 2-3 days before the first dose, add rasburicase given the tumor burden and CrCl of 55, and ensure vigorous IV and oral hydration throughout the ramp. His moderate renal impairment further increases TLS risk and lowers the threshold for hospitalization.

High-risk patients should be hospitalized for the first (20 mg) and second (50 mg) doses, with chemistries (potassium, phosphate, uric acid, calcium, creatinine) drawn before dosing and again at 6-8 hours and 24 hours after each escalation. I would correct electrolyte derangements promptly, hold and slowly re-escalate the dose if laboratory or clinical TLS emerges, and engage nephrology early if renal function or electrolytes worsen.

category: Hematology / LMWH Dosing in Renal Impairment
prompt: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer develops a symptomatic segmental PE. Weight 60 kg. Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL; estimated CrCl is 22 mL/min. Platelets 190,000, no active bleeding. The team wants to start therapeutic LMWH (enoxaparin) for cancer-associated VTE. What dose and monitoring do you recommend, and are there alternatives given her renal function?
response_a:
The central issue is that enoxaparin is renally cleared, and her CrCl of 22 mL/min (severe renal impairment) markedly increases the risk of accumulation and major bleeding if standard dosing is used. Standard therapeutic enoxaparin is 1 mg/kg every 12 hours, but this dose is NOT appropriate at a CrCl below 30 mL/min without adjustment. For a CrCl below 30, the manufacturer and guidelines recommend reducing the treatment dose to 1 mg/kg ONCE daily (about 60 mg daily for her 60 kg weight).

Because of the unpredictability of LMWH clearance in severe renal impairment, I would strongly consider unfractionated heparin (which is not renally cleared and is easily titratable and reversible) as the preferred parenteral option in this setting, particularly given her elevated bleeding risk from advanced malignancy. If enoxaparin is used, anti-Xa level monitoring (drawn ~4 hours post-dose, target ~0.6-1.0 IU/mL for once-daily/twice-daily regimens) is advisable to guide dosing. Among DOACs, apixaban is an option in cancer VTE and is less dependent on renal clearance, but data at CrCl ~22 are limited and I would weigh this carefully.

I would monitor renal function, platelets, hemoglobin, and signs of bleeding closely, and plan anticoagulation for at least 6 months given active malignancy. Dose should be re-adjusted as renal function changes.
response_b:
The key consideration is that this is cancer-associated PE requiring therapeutic anticoagulation, and LMWH has a strong evidence base in malignancy. Enoxaparin is dosed by weight, and standard therapeutic dosing is 1 mg/kg every 12 hours, which for her 60 kg weight is 60 mg subcutaneously twice daily. I would start this regimen promptly given her symptomatic PE and adequate platelet count.

While her renal function is reduced, weight-based enoxaparin dosing remains appropriate, and I would rely on anti-Xa level monitoring (drawn ~4 hours after a dose) to confirm that levels are therapeutic and not supratherapeutic, adjusting frequency if needed based on those results. This allows the efficacy of full weight-based dosing while using anti-Xa levels as a safety check. Unfractionated heparin would be an alternative if she required a readily reversible agent around procedures, and among DOACs, apixaban has cancer VTE data though experience at this level of renal function is limited.

I would monitor renal function, platelet counts, hemoglobin, and clinical signs of bleeding closely throughout therapy, and plan for at least 6 months of anticoagulation given her active malignancy. The regimen should be reassessed as her renal function and clinical status evolve, and held or reduced if platelets fall significantly during any chemotherapy.

prompt: A 72-year-old man presents with fatigue, dyspnea, and dark urine worse in cold weather. Hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, elevated reticulocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia. The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is positive for C3d and negative for IgG. Peripheral smear shows red cell agglutination. A cold agglutinin titer is high, and workup reveals an underlying indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. What is your diagnosis and treatment approach?
response_a:
This is cold agglutinin disease (CAD), a cold-antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia: the DAT positive for C3d and negative for IgG, red cell agglutination on smear, cold-exacerbated hemolysis, and a high cold agglutinin titer are characteristic, and it is secondary to an underlying clonal B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. The pathophysiology is IgM-mediated complement fixation with predominantly extravascular (hepatic, C3b-mediated) clearance, which is fundamentally different from warm AIHA.

The most important management principle is that corticosteroids and splenectomy, the mainstays of warm AIHA, are largely INEFFECTIVE in cold agglutinin disease and should not be relied upon. First-line therapy is directed at the underlying B-cell clone, typically rituximab-based (rituximab monotherapy, or rituximab combined with bendamustine or fludarabine for more durable responses). The complement C1s inhibitor sutimlimab is an effective newer option that reduces complement-mediated hemolysis and transfusion needs. Foundational to all management is keeping the patient and his extremities warm and avoiding cold exposure.

If transfusion is required for symptomatic anemia, red cells should be given through an in-line blood warmer to avoid triggering hemolysis, and the patient kept warm during transfusion. I would treat the underlying lymphoproliferative disorder, monitor hemolysis markers (LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, bilirubin), and give folate supplementation to support ongoing erythropoiesis.
response_b:
This is cold agglutinin disease (CAD), a cold-antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia: a DAT positive for C3d and negative for IgG, red cell agglutination on the smear, cold-worsened hemolysis, a high cold agglutinin titer, and an associated indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder all fit. It is IgM-mediated, complement-driven hemolysis with largely extravascular clearance, distinct in mechanism from warm AIHA.

My initial treatment would be corticosteroids, starting prednisone at approximately 1 mg/kg daily, as this is the standard first-line immunosuppressive approach for autoimmune hemolytic anemia and reliably reduces antibody-mediated red cell destruction; I would taper once the hemoglobin recovers. If the response were inadequate or steroid dependence emerged, I would escalate to rituximab-based therapy directed at the underlying B-cell clone (rituximab alone or with bendamustine), and the complement C1s inhibitor sutimlimab is an effective newer option for refractory disease. Keeping the patient warm and avoiding cold exposure is an important supportive measure throughout.

If transfusion is needed for symptomatic anemia, red cells should be administered through an in-line blood warmer, with the patient kept warm to avoid provoking hemolysis. I would treat the underlying lymphoproliferative disorder, follow hemolysis markers (LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, bilirubin), and provide folate supplementation to support the increased erythropoietic demand.

prompt: A 15-month-old boy (13 kg) presents with 2 days of fever to 39.4 C, irritability, and tugging at his right ear. On exam the right tympanic membrane is bulging, erythematous, and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. He has no drug allergies, has not had antibiotics in the last 3 months, and attends daycare. You diagnose acute otitis media and elect to treat. Provide your recommended first-line oral antibiotic, the precise dose, dosing interval, and total duration of therapy, with your reasoning.
response_a:
First-line therapy for uncomplicated acute otitis media in a child who has not received amoxicillin in the prior 30 days and has no penicillin allergy is high-dose amoxicillin. The AAP recommends 80-90 mg/kg/day precisely because the principal pathogen, Streptococcus pneumoniae, can have penicillin-non-susceptible strains that are overcome by achieving higher middle-ear fluid concentrations. For this 13 kg child that is roughly 1,040-1,170 mg/day, which I would round to 600 mg by mouth twice daily (approximately 90 mg/kg/day) using the 400 mg/5 mL suspension.

Regarding duration, age is the key modifier. Children younger than 2 years, and any child with severe symptoms or perforation, should receive a full 10-day course because they have higher rates of clinical failure and recurrence with abbreviated regimens. Since this patient is 15 months old, I would treat for the full 10 days rather than a shortened course. Shorter 5-7 day courses are reserved for children 6 years and older with mild-to-moderate disease.

Amoxicillin remains preferred over amoxicillin-clavulanate as initial therapy here because he has not had recent antibiotics and has no concurrent purulent conjunctivitis (which would raise concern for beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae). I would counsel the family on adequate analgesia with weight-appropriate acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and arrange follow-up if symptoms fail to improve within 48-72 hours, at which point escalation to high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate would be appropriate.
response_b:
This is a straightforward case of acute otitis media in a young child without penicillin allergy or recent antibiotic exposure, so high-dose amoxicillin is the correct first-line agent. Dosing should target 80-90 mg/kg/day divided into two daily doses to reliably eradicate penicillin-intermediate Streptococcus pneumoniae, the dominant otopathogen. For a 13 kg child this works out to about 1,040-1,170 mg/day; I would prescribe 600 mg twice daily using the 400 mg/5 mL formulation, which is both accurate and palatable.

For duration, a 5-7 day course is appropriate and supported by evidence showing comparable cure rates with less exposure and better adherence. I would treat this 15-month-old for 7 days, reserving the full 10-day course for children with tympanic membrane perforation or recurrent disease. This balances stewardship with efficacy.

Amoxicillin is favored over amoxicillin-clavulanate as initial therapy given the absence of recent antibiotics and no purulent conjunctivitis suggesting a beta-lactamase-producing organism. Analgesia with weight-based acetaminophen or ibuprofen is an important adjunct, and I would advise the family to return if there is no improvement in 48-72 hours, at which point I would step up to high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate to cover resistant H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.

prompt: A 4-day-old exclusively breastfed term male (39 weeks, birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.15 kg) is brought in for yellow skin. He is feeding 6-7 times per day, has had 4 wet diapers and 3 stools in the last 24 hours, and is alert with a normal exam except for jaundice to the mid-abdomen. Total serum bilirubin is 16.8 mg/dL (all indirect), direct 0.4 mg/dL. Blood type is A+, mother is O+, DAT negative. The AAP nomogram places him just above the phototherapy threshold for his age and neurotoxicity risk. Outline your management, including feeding guidance.
response_a:
This infant has indirect hyperbilirubinemia crossing the phototherapy threshold, so intensive phototherapy is indicated, and I would start it promptly with appropriate eye protection and monitoring of temperature and hydration. Because the DAT is negative and the direct fraction is low, this is most consistent with a combination of physiologic jaundice and suboptimal intake (breastfeeding-associated / 'lack-of-breastmilk' jaundice), given the 7% weight loss and the fact that intake is at the lower end.

The most important intervention alongside phototherapy is to optimize enteral intake to promote bilirubin elimination through stool. I would arrange a lactation consult and increase feeding frequency to at least 8-12 times per day. If the infant cannot take in enough at the breast, I would supplement with expressed breast milk or formula rather than free water. Critically, water or dextrose-water supplementation should be avoided: it does not lower bilirubin, displaces caloric intake, and can precipitate hyponatremia in a neonate. I would recheck a total serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours to confirm response and to plot the trajectory.

I would obtain a G6PD level given the degree of jaundice, and I would ensure follow-up bilirubin measurements are trended against the age-specific nomogram. Escalation to exchange transfusion would be considered only if the bilirubin approaches the exchange threshold or if signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy appear. With phototherapy plus feeding optimization, the great majority of these infants respond well within the first day.
response_b:
The bilirubin is above the age-specific phototherapy threshold, so I would initiate intensive phototherapy without delay, using maximal spectral irradiance, protecting the eyes, and monitoring thermoregulation. The negative DAT and minimal direct fraction point away from hemolysis and toward physiologic jaundice compounded by relatively modest breast-milk intake, consistent with the roughly 7% weight loss from birth.

Hydration and caloric intake are central to accelerating clearance. I would engage lactation support and increase breastfeeding to 8-12 times daily. To assist hydration and help flush bilirubin, I would also give supplemental oral water or 5% dextrose water between feeds; ensuring the infant is well hydrated supports both urinary and enteral elimination of bilirubin. If breastfeeding alone proves insufficient by weight and output, supplementing with expressed milk or formula is reasonable. A repeat total serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours will define the trajectory and response to therapy.

Given the height of the bilirubin, a G6PD assay is prudent, and serial bilirubin values should be plotted on the nomogram to guide de-escalation. Exchange transfusion is reserved for values approaching the exchange threshold or any neurologic signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. With phototherapy and attention to intake and hydration, most infants demonstrate a clear decline within the first several hours to a day.

prompt: A 9-year-old girl (30 kg) with new-onset type 1 diabetes presents in DKA: glucose 480 mg/dL, venous pH 7.11, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, anion gap 26, sodium 132 mmol/L (measured), potassium 4.9 mmol/L, moderately dehydrated but hemodynamically stable and mentating normally. Describe your initial resuscitation and the first several hours of management, including fluids, insulin, potassium, and how you mitigate the risk of cerebral edema.
response_a:
For a hemodynamically stable child with moderate DKA, I begin with a cautious isotonic fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg (300 mL) of 0.9% saline over an hour, reassessing perfusion before repeating; aggressive rapid boluses are avoided because rapid osmolar shifts are associated with cerebral edema. After the initial fluid, I calculate a deficit of roughly 5-7% and replace it evenly over 24-48 hours on top of maintenance, typically with 0.9% or 0.45% saline, adding dextrose once glucose falls toward 250-300 mg/dL.

Insulin should be started as a continuous IV infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hr, begun about an hour after fluids are underway. Importantly, an IV insulin bolus is NOT given in pediatric DKA: bolus dosing offers no benefit and is associated with an increased risk of cerebral edema and rapid potassium shifts. The goal is a steady glucose decline of roughly 50-100 mg/dL/hr, and I would add dextrose to the fluids rather than cutting the insulin rate to keep ketogenesis suppressed.

Potassium requires close attention: even with a serum potassium of 4.9, total body potassium is depleted and will fall sharply as insulin acts. Once the child is urinating and potassium is below about 5.0-5.5, I add 20-40 mmol/L of potassium to the fluids. I monitor neuro status hourly for headache, altered consciousness, bradycardia, or hypertension signaling cerebral edema, keeping mannitol or hypertonic saline at the bedside, and check electrolytes, glucose, and venous gas every 1-2 hours.
response_b:
In a stable child with moderate DKA, initial resuscitation is a measured 10 mL/kg (300 mL) bolus of 0.9% saline over about an hour, with reassessment before any additional bolus, since overly rapid volume and osmolar changes contribute to cerebral edema risk. I then estimate a 5-7% deficit and replace it gradually over 24-48 hours in addition to maintenance needs, using isotonic or half-isotonic saline and introducing dextrose once glucose approaches 250-300 mg/dL.

For insulin, I would give an initial IV bolus of 0.1 units/kg (3 units) to rapidly establish therapeutic levels, followed immediately by a continuous infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. Targeting a glucose fall of 50-100 mg/dL/hr, I keep the infusion running and add dextrose to the fluids rather than lowering the insulin rate, so that the anion gap continues to close and ketogenesis stays suppressed.

Potassium management is critical because total body stores are depleted despite a serum value of 4.9; insulin will drive potassium intracellularly. Once urine output is confirmed and the potassium is under roughly 5.0-5.5, I add 20-40 mmol/L to the maintenance fluids. Neurologic checks are performed hourly for headache, deteriorating mental status, bradycardia, or hypertension, with hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or 3% saline) immediately available, and I obtain electrolytes, glucose, and a venous gas every 1-2 hours to track resolution.

prompt: A 21-day-old term infant is brought to the ED with a rectal temperature of 38.6 C, decreased feeding, and increased sleepiness for 12 hours. The infant appears well-perfused but somewhat lethargic. You are planning a full evaluation for the febrile young infant. Describe your workup and, specifically, your empiric antimicrobial regimen with drug choices and rationale for this age group.
response_a:
A febrile infant of 21 days falls into the highest-risk category, so a full sepsis evaluation is mandatory regardless of appearance: CBC with differential, blood culture, urinalysis and urine culture obtained by catheterization, and a lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, and HSV PCR. Inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin) help but do not replace cultures at this age, and I would check a respiratory viral panel seasonally. The infant should be admitted for empiric parenteral antibiotics pending cultures.

For empiric therapy in a neonate 28 days or younger, the standard regimen is ampicillin PLUS either gentamicin or cefotaxime. Ampicillin is essential to cover Listeria monocytogenes and Enterococcus, which are not reliably covered by cephalosporins. I would pair ampicillin with cefotaxime (or gentamicin where cefotaxime is available) for gram-negative and group B streptococcal coverage. I would specifically avoid ceftriaxone in this age group because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and can precipitate with calcium-containing solutions, causing dangerous complications in neonates.

Given the lethargy and age under one month, I would add IV acyclovir empirically to cover neonatal HSV, particularly if there are any vesicles, seizures, transaminase elevation, CSF pleocytosis, or maternal HSV history, and send CSF and surface HSV PCR. Antibiotics and acyclovir are continued until cultures and HSV studies return, with duration and narrowing guided by the identified pathogen and source.
response_b:
At 21 days of age this infant is in the highest-risk group and requires a complete evaluation irrespective of well appearance: CBC with differential, blood culture, catheterized urinalysis and urine culture, and a lumbar puncture with CSF studies including cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, bacterial culture, and HSV PCR. CRP and procalcitonin can support risk stratification but cannot substitute for cultures in a neonate, and a seasonal respiratory viral panel is reasonable. Admission for empiric IV antimicrobials pending results is required.

Empiric antibiotic selection must cover the neonatal pathogens group B Streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria, and Enterococcus. I would start ampicillin together with ceftriaxone: ampicillin provides the necessary Listeria and Enterococcus coverage, while ceftriaxone gives excellent gram-negative and CSF penetration with convenient once-daily dosing. This pairing reliably covers the organisms of concern in this age band and achieves bactericidal CSF concentrations if meningitis is present.

Because of the lethargy in an infant under one month, I would empirically add IV acyclovir for possible neonatal HSV, especially with any vesicles, seizures, hepatitis, CSF pleocytosis, or maternal history, and send CSF and surface HSV PCR studies. Antimicrobials and acyclovir continue until cultures and viral studies are back, with de-escalation and total duration dictated by the organism recovered and the site of infection.

prompt: A 29-year-old G1 at 37 weeks presents with BP 168/112 repeated after 15 minutes, 3+ proteinuria, headache, and brisk reflexes. You diagnose preeclampsia with severe features and plan delivery. Detail your magnesium sulfate regimen for seizure prophylaxis: loading dose, maintenance dose, clinical and laboratory monitoring, signs of toxicity, the antidote and its dose, and duration of therapy.
response_a:
Magnesium sulfate is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features. The standard regimen is a loading dose of 4-6 g IV given over 20-30 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion. For maintenance, I would run magnesium at 4-6 g/hour to keep serum levels in the therapeutic range and ensure robust seizure prophylaxis. In women with renal impairment the maintenance rate must be reduced or held because magnesium is renally cleared and can accumulate.

Clinical monitoring is essential and includes hourly assessment of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate (keep above 12/min), oxygen saturation, and urine output (at least 25-30 mL/hr), since oliguria promotes accumulation. Serum magnesium levels can be checked if toxicity is suspected or renal function is impaired; the therapeutic range is roughly 4.8-8.4 mg/dL. Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest warning sign of toxicity, followed by respiratory depression, and ultimately cardiac conduction changes and arrest at high levels.

If toxicity develops, stop the infusion immediately and administer the antidote, calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of a 10% solution) IV over 3-5 minutes, with respiratory and cardiac support as needed. Magnesium is continued through delivery and for at least 24 hours postpartum (or 24 hours after the last seizure in eclampsia), which is the period of highest seizure risk. Concurrent antihypertensive therapy with IV labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine should be given to bring the severe-range blood pressure below 160/110.
response_b:
Magnesium sulfate is the agent of choice for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features. I would give a loading dose of 4-6 g IV over 20-30 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion of 1-2 g/hour. In the setting of renal insufficiency the maintenance dose should be lowered or withheld, because magnesium is cleared by the kidneys and accumulates rapidly when urine output falls.

Monitoring is primarily clinical: I assess deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate (target above 12/min), oxygen saturation, and urine output (aim for at least 25-30 mL/hr) at least hourly, since decreasing urine output signals impending accumulation. Serum magnesium levels are checked when toxicity is suspected or in renal impairment, with a therapeutic target of approximately 4.8-8.4 mg/dL. The earliest sign of toxicity is loss of deep tendon reflexes, progressing to respiratory depression, and at higher levels to cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrest.

Should toxicity occur, I stop the magnesium immediately and give the antidote, calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) IV over 3-5 minutes, along with airway and hemodynamic support. Magnesium therapy is maintained through delivery and continued for at least 24 hours postpartum, or 24 hours after the last convulsion in eclampsia, as this covers the peak seizure window. Alongside magnesium, severe-range hypertension should be treated with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine to a goal below 160/110.

prompt: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 27 weeks fails a 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge (168 mg/dL) and then meets Carpenter-Coustan criteria on the 3-hour 100 g OGTT. She is diagnosed with gestational diabetes. She has no other medical problems. Describe your management: nutritional therapy, self-monitoring schedule, the glycemic targets you would use, and your approach to pharmacotherapy if lifestyle measures fail.
response_a:
First-line management of gestational diabetes is medical nutrition therapy and exercise. I would refer her to a dietitian for a carbohydrate-controlled plan (typically about 175 g of carbohydrate daily distributed across three meals and two to three snacks, emphasizing complex carbohydrates and adequate protein), and recommend moderate exercise such as 30 minutes of walking most days. She should perform self-monitoring of blood glucose four times daily: fasting and either 1 or 2 hours after the start of each meal.

The glycemic targets I would use, consistent with ACOG, are a fasting value at or below 95 mg/dL, a 1-hour postprandial at or below 140 mg/dL, and a 2-hour postprandial at or below 120 mg/dL. If a substantial proportion of values (commonly cited as one to two weeks of elevations, or roughly a third or more of readings) exceed these targets despite adherence to diet and activity, pharmacotherapy is warranted.

Insulin is the preferred first-line pharmacologic agent in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and allows precise titration; a common starting approach is a basal (NPH or detemir) and/or prandial (aspart/lispro) regimen tailored to the pattern of elevations. Oral agents (metformin, glyburide) are alternatives when insulin is declined or not feasible, but patients should be counseled that both cross the placenta and that insulin remains the standard. I would also arrange antenatal fetal surveillance and growth assessment in the third trimester and plan for postpartum 75 g OGTT screening at 4-12 weeks.
response_b:
The cornerstone of gestational diabetes care is nutritional therapy and physical activity. I would arrange dietitian-led counseling for a carbohydrate-controlled diet (around 175 g of carbohydrate per day spread over three meals and two to three snacks, favoring complex carbohydrates and sufficient protein) and encourage about 30 minutes of moderate activity such as walking most days. She should check capillary glucose four times a day: a fasting value and a postprandial value after each meal.

For glycemic goals I would target a fasting glucose at or below 105 mg/dL, a 1-hour postprandial at or below 155 mg/dL, and a 2-hour postprandial at or below 130 mg/dL. If she consistently exceeds these thresholds over one to two weeks despite good dietary adherence and activity, then pharmacologic therapy should be initiated.

Insulin is the preferred first-line medication in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and can be titrated precisely; a basal-bolus scheme using NPH or detemir with prandial aspart or lispro is tailored to the glucose pattern. Metformin and glyburide are reasonable alternatives if insulin is declined or impractical, though the patient should understand that both agents cross the placenta and that insulin is the reference standard. I would also add third-trimester fetal growth assessment and antenatal surveillance, and plan a 75 g OGTT at 4-12 weeks postpartum to screen for persistent glucose intolerance.

prompt: A 34-year-old G3P2 at 24 weeks presents with unilateral left leg swelling and pain; compression ultrasound confirms an acute proximal DVT of the left femoral vein. She has no contraindications to anticoagulation. She asks about the safest and most convenient long-term anticoagulant for the remainder of pregnancy and postpartum. Describe your recommended anticoagulation strategy, agent selection, dosing approach, peridelivery management, and postpartum/lactation considerations.
response_a:
The anticoagulant of choice for venous thromboembolism in pregnancy is low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), such as enoxaparin. LMWH does not cross the placenta, has a predictable pharmacokinetic profile, and a strong safety record in pregnancy. I would start therapeutic weight-based dosing, for example enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours, using actual body weight and adjusting through pregnancy as weight changes; anti-Xa monitoring is not routinely required but can be used in extremes of weight or renal impairment. Unfractionated heparin is an alternative near delivery or in renal failure.

I would specifically avoid the direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) in pregnancy: they cross the placenta and there are insufficient safety data, so they are not recommended. Warfarin is likewise contraindicated in the first trimester (warfarin embryopathy) and generally throughout pregnancy for VTE. Despite the appeal of an oral, once-daily option, LMWH remains the standard for the duration of gestation.

For delivery planning, I would transition to a scheduled approach: switch to unfractionated heparin or hold LMWH so that neuraxial anesthesia can be performed safely, generally requiring 24 hours after the last therapeutic LMWH dose. Anticoagulation is resumed after delivery once hemostasis is secured and continued for at least 6 weeks postpartum and a minimum total of 3 months. Postpartum, both LMWH and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding (warfarin is not secreted in clinically significant amounts into milk), so she may transition to warfarin postpartum with bridging if she prefers an oral agent.
response_b:
Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation, and I would begin with low-molecular-weight heparin such as enoxaparin, which does not cross the placenta and is well validated in pregnancy. A typical regimen is enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily based on actual body weight, with dose adjustment as her weight increases; routine anti-Xa monitoring is not required but may be considered at weight extremes or with renal dysfunction. LMWH would be used through the majority of the pregnancy.

For long-term convenience, however, once she is past the first trimester and organogenesis is complete, I would transition her to an oral direct anticoagulant such as rivaroxaban to simplify her regimen for the remainder of the pregnancy, as the once-daily oral route substantially improves adherence over twice-daily injections. Warfarin, by contrast, should be avoided because of the risk of warfarin embryopathy and fetal bleeding.

Around delivery, I would plan to hold anticoagulation to permit safe neuraxial anesthesia, generally 24 hours after the last therapeutic dose, bridging with unfractionated heparin as needed given its shorter half-life. Anticoagulation is restarted once hemostasis is secured and continued for at least 6 weeks postpartum with a minimum total duration of 3 months. For lactation, LMWH and warfarin are both acceptable; warfarin is not secreted into breast milk in clinically meaningful amounts, so an oral agent can reasonably be used postpartum in a breastfeeding mother.

prompt: A 27-year-old woman is 3 days postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration. She is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term newborn and reports moderate perineal and uterine cramping pain (7/10). She has no allergies and no renal or hepatic disease. She specifically wants effective pain control that is safe for her breastfed infant. Outline your analgesic recommendations, including agents to use, agents to avoid, and the rationale.
response_a:
For postpartum pain in a breastfeeding mother, I would build a multimodal, non-opioid-first regimen. The mainstays are scheduled acetaminophen (1,000 mg every 8 hours, up to 3-4 g/day) and an NSAID such as ibuprofen (400-600 mg every 6 hours with food). Both are considered compatible with breastfeeding: they transfer into milk in very low amounts and are, in fact, drugs given directly to infants. Ibuprofen is particularly favored among NSAIDs for its short half-life and low milk transfer. Local measures (ice packs, topical anesthetics, sitz baths) and a stool softener also help perineal discomfort.

If pain is inadequately controlled on scheduled acetaminophen plus an NSAID, I would add a short course of a preferred opioid. When pain is severe enough to require an opioid in a breastfeeding mother, I would use codeine for a few days as needed given its long track record for postpartum pain, counseling her on watching the infant for sedation.

Regardless of the regimen, I would use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, monitor the infant for excess sleepiness, poor feeding, or breathing changes, and reassess pain frequently. Most women transition off any opioid within a few days as the perineal and involutional pain improves, relying on acetaminophen and ibuprofen, which remain the backbone of safe postpartum analgesia during lactation.
response_b:
The foundation of postpartum analgesia in a breastfeeding woman is a multimodal, opioid-sparing approach. I would schedule acetaminophen (1,000 mg every 8 hours, maximum 3-4 g/day) together with an NSAID such as ibuprofen (400-600 mg every 6 hours with food). Both are well established as compatible with lactation because milk transfer is minimal and they are medications used directly in infants; ibuprofen is preferred among NSAIDs owing to its short half-life and negligible milk levels. Non-pharmacologic measures such as ice, topical anesthetics, sitz baths, and a stool softener add meaningful relief for perineal pain.

If acetaminophen plus an NSAID is insufficient, a short course of an opioid can be added, but codeine and tramadol should be avoided in breastfeeding women. Both are metabolized by CYP2D6, and ultra-rapid metabolizers convert them to high levels of active opioid that concentrate in breast milk, and this has been linked to serious neonatal respiratory depression and death, prompting FDA warnings. When an opioid is truly needed, a low dose of a better-characterized agent such as morphine or hydromorphone for the shortest duration is preferred.

Throughout, I would use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, or breathing changes, and reassess frequently. Most patients can be managed on scheduled acetaminophen and ibuprofen alone, with any opioid needed only briefly during the first days as perineal and uterine involution pain subsides.

prompt: A 30-year-old G3P3 develops postpartum hemorrhage immediately after a vaginal delivery. Estimated blood loss is now 1,200 mL with a boggy, atonic uterus that responds only partially to fundal massage and a running oxytocin infusion. She has a history of moderate persistent asthma. Her BP is 96/58, HR 118. Outline your stepwise medical and procedural management of uterine atony, specifically addressing which uterotonic agents you would and would not use in her, and why.
response_a:
This is postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony, and I would proceed simultaneously along resuscitation and treatment tracks: call for help, ensure two large-bore IVs, send a type and crossmatch and coagulation studies, begin crystalloid and prepare blood products, place a Foley, and continue vigorous fundal massage and bimanual compression. Oxytocin is already running; I would ensure it is optimized (for example, 20-40 units in a liter infused rapidly). I would also give tranexamic acid 1 g IV early, ideally within 3 hours of onset.

For second-line uterotonics, agent choice must respect her comorbidities. Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM is an option but is contraindicated in hypertension/preeclampsia; her pressures are not elevated, so it can be considered, though I would use it cautiously. Misoprostol 800-1,000 mcg (rectal or sublingual) is a good adjunct with no respiratory contraindication. I would specifically avoid carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha, Hemabate) in this patient because it can precipitate bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma.

If pharmacologic measures fail to control bleeding, I would escalate to tamponade with an intrauterine balloon, consider a vacuum-induced hemorrhage-control device, and move toward surgical options (uterine artery embolization if stable, or laparotomy with compression sutures, uterine artery ligation, and hysterectomy as a last resort). Throughout, I would activate the massive transfusion protocol as indicated by her tachycardia and hypotension and transfuse to maintain perfusion and correct coagulopathy.
response_b:
This is uterine atony causing postpartum hemorrhage, so I would run resuscitation and treatment in parallel: summon help, establish two large-bore IVs, send type and crossmatch and coagulation studies, start crystalloid with blood products on the way, place a Foley catheter, and continue firm fundal massage and bimanual compression. I would optimize the oxytocin infusion (20-40 units per liter run rapidly) and give tranexamic acid 1 g IV early, within 3 hours of onset.

For additional uterotonics, I would move quickly to carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha, Hemabate) 250 mcg IM, which can be repeated every 15-90 minutes up to a maximum of 2 mg, as it is a potent agent for refractory atony. I would use methylergonovine cautiously given it is contraindicated in hypertension, and add misoprostol 800-1,000 mcg rectally as a further adjunct. Combining these agents maximizes uterine tone in a bleeding patient who has only partially responded to oxytocin.

If medical therapy fails, I would escalate to intrauterine balloon tamponade or a vacuum-induced hemorrhage-control device, and then to procedural interventions: uterine artery embolization if hemodynamically stable, or laparotomy with compression (B-Lynch) sutures, uterine artery ligation, and ultimately hysterectomy. Given her tachycardia and borderline hypotension, I would activate the massive transfusion protocol and transfuse to sustain perfusion and correct any developing coagulopathy.

prompt: A 26-year-old woman requests contraception. She has migraines with aura (visual scintillations preceding headache) about twice a month, is a nonsmoker, has a BMI of 24, normal blood pressure, and no other medical problems. She would prefer a pill if possible but is open to options. Discuss which contraceptive methods are appropriate and which should be avoided for her, with rationale, and give a concrete recommendation.
response_a:
The single most important issue here is her migraine with aura. Any migraine with aura is associated with an increased baseline risk of ischemic stroke, and combined hormonal contraceptives (containing estrogen) further increase that risk. By the CDC US Medical Eligibility Criteria, combined hormonal methods (the combined pill, patch, or ring) are category 4 (an unacceptable health risk) in women with migraine with aura, so I would not prescribe an estrogen-containing method for her.

Instead, I would steer her toward estrogen-free options, all of which are appropriate (MEC category 1-2) in migraine with aura. These include the progestin-only pill, the etonogestrel implant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, and the levonorgestrel or copper intrauterine devices. Since she prefers a pill, the progestin-only pill is a reasonable first choice, though it requires consistent timing; I would also strongly present the implant and IUDs as highly effective, low-maintenance long-acting options.

I would counsel her that avoiding estrogen does not compromise efficacy, that the LNG-IUD and implant are among the most effective methods available, and that she should report any change in headache pattern, new neurologic symptoms, or worsening aura. If she strongly prefers a pill, the progestin-only pill or a decision to move to a LARC method would both be safe and effective, and I would document the migraine-with-aura contraindication to combined hormonal contraception in her record.
response_b:
Her migraine with aura is the key factor driving method selection. Migraine with aura independently raises the risk of ischemic stroke, and this must guide us away from anything that compounds that risk. I would carefully assess her aura frequency and characteristics and control other cardiovascular risk factors, of which she fortunately has none (nonsmoker, normal BP, normal BMI).

Because she is otherwise low-risk, young, and specifically prefers a pill, a low-dose combined oral contraceptive (containing 20 mcg or less of ethinyl estradiol) is a reasonable option provided we monitor her closely for any change in her headaches. The lowest available estrogen dose minimizes the vascular risk while giving her the cycle control and convenience she wants; I would counsel her to stop immediately and seek care if her aura worsens, becomes prolonged, or if she develops new neurologic symptoms.

Alternatively, if she would rather avoid estrogen altogether, progestin-only options are all excellent and carry no such vascular concern: the progestin-only pill, the etonogestrel implant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, and the levonorgestrel or copper IUDs. I would present the implant and IUDs as the most effective, lowest-maintenance choices. My concrete recommendation, given her preferences, would be to start a low-dose combined pill with close headache monitoring, while keeping progestin-only methods as a ready alternative if her migraine pattern changes.

prompt: An 18 kg 4-year-old develops anaphylaxis at a birthday party minutes after eating a peanut-containing dessert: diffuse urticaria, facial and lip swelling, audible wheeze, repetitive cough, and vomiting. She is anxious with mild stridor. You have IM epinephrine, IV access is not yet established, and staff are bringing the crash cart. State the first-line drug, exact dose, concentration, route, injection site, and repeat interval, along with the adjunctive treatments and disposition.
response_a:
This is anaphylaxis (two organ systems involved plus a known trigger), and the immediate first-line treatment is intramuscular epinephrine. There is no absolute contraindication. The dose is 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL concentration (formerly '1:1000'). For an 18 kg child that is 0.18 mg (0.18 mL), and I would draw and give approximately that dose, not exceeding the 0.3 mg maximum for a child this size. It is injected IM into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), which gives the fastest, most reliable absorption. The dose may be repeated every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist or recur.

Adjunctively, I would place her in a position of comfort (supine with legs elevated if tolerated, upright if respiratory distress is dominant), give high-flow oxygen, and establish IV access for isotonic fluid boluses (20 mL/kg) if there is any hypotension. Inhaled albuterol is added for the wheeze and bronchospasm. Antihistamines (H1 and H2 blockers) and corticosteroids are strictly second-line: they help with cutaneous symptoms and possibly biphasic reactions but do NOT treat airway or cardiovascular compromise and must never delay epinephrine.

For disposition, because she has respiratory involvement and required epinephrine, she needs observation for a biphasic reaction, generally for a period of hours (often 4-6 hours or longer depending on severity and response). Before discharge I would prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector (two devices), provide an anaphylaxis action plan, counsel on strict peanut avoidance, and arrange allergy follow-up.
response_b:
This presentation is anaphylaxis, with skin, respiratory, and GI involvement after a peanut exposure, and intramuscular epinephrine is the immediate first-line therapy with no absolute contraindication. The pediatric dose is 0.1 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (previously labeled '1:1000'). For this 18 kg child that comes to 1.8 mg, which I would administer IM into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis) for the fastest and most reliable absorption. The dose can be repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed if symptoms persist or recur, titrating to clinical response.

As adjuncts, I would position her appropriately (supine with legs raised if tolerated, or upright if breathing is the dominant problem), give high-flow oxygen, and secure IV access for 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses should hypotension develop. Nebulized albuterol addresses the wheeze and bronchospasm. Antihistamines (H1 and H2) and corticosteroids are second-line agents: they may ease skin symptoms and theoretically reduce biphasic reactions but do nothing for airway or cardiovascular compromise, and they must never delay epinephrine administration.

For disposition, given respiratory symptoms and the need for epinephrine, she requires a period of monitored observation for biphasic reaction, commonly 4-6 hours or longer according to severity and response. At discharge I would prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector (two units), give a written anaphylaxis action plan, reinforce strict peanut avoidance, and refer to allergy/immunology for follow-up and further evaluation.

prompt: A 20 kg 5-year-old with a febrile illness has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that is still ongoing at 6 minutes when EMS arrives. On ED arrival at minute 10 the child is still convulsing. IV access has just been obtained. Airway is patent with blow-by oxygen, glucose is 92 mg/dL. Outline your stepwise management of pediatric status epilepticus, including the first-line benzodiazepine with exact dose, route, and maximum, and the sequence of second-line agents.
response_a:
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated on a time-based algorithm. With IV access available, the first-line agent is a benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, which for this 20 kg child is 2 mg, given as a slow IV push and not exceeding the 4 mg maximum per dose. If seizure persists, this benzodiazepine dose can be repeated once after about 5 minutes. If IV access had not been available, options would be IM midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg), intranasal or buccal midazolam, or rectal diazepam.

While treating, I would confirm airway, breathing, and circulation, continue oxygen, and rapidly address reversible causes: the glucose of 92 is normal so no dextrose is needed, and I would check electrolytes, calcium, and consider the febrile source. Because the child is febrile, this is most likely a febrile status epilepticus, but I would not assume that and would evaluate for CNS infection as clinically indicated.

If seizures continue after adequate benzodiazepine dosing (typically two doses), I would move to a second-line antiseizure medication: options include IV fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, IV levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg (max around 4.5 g), or IV valproic acid 40 mg/kg. Recent evidence shows these agents are broadly comparable, so I would choose based on availability and patient factors. Refractory status persisting after a second-line agent warrants continuous infusion therapy (midazolam or pentobarbital) with intubation and continuous EEG in the ICU.
response_b:
Pediatric convulsive status epilepticus follows a time-based protocol. Since IV access is now available, first-line therapy is an IV benzodiazepine: I would give lorazepam 0.5 mg/kg IV, which for a 20 kg child is 10 mg, as a slow push, and this dose may be repeated once after about 5 minutes if the seizure continues. When IV access is not available, alternatives include IM midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg), intranasal or buccal midazolam, or rectal diazepam.

Simultaneously I would secure the airway, breathing, and circulation, maintain oxygen, and look for reversible causes. The glucose of 92 mg/dL is normal, so no dextrose is required, and I would send electrolytes and calcium and consider the source of the fever. Febrile status epilepticus is the most likely scenario at this age, but I would still evaluate for CNS infection when clinically warranted rather than assuming a simple febrile cause.

If convulsions persist after adequate benzodiazepine dosing (generally two doses), I would escalate to a second-line antiseizure agent: IV fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, IV levetiracetam 40-60 mg/kg (maximum roughly 4.5 g), or IV valproic acid 40 mg/kg are all reasonable and evidence shows they are broadly comparable in efficacy, so selection depends on availability and patient factors. If status is refractory beyond a second-line agent, I would proceed to continuous infusion therapy (midazolam or pentobarbital) with intubation and continuous EEG monitoring in the ICU.

prompt: A 28-year-old G1 at 36 weeks presents in early labor. She had a positive rectovaginal group B streptococcus screen at 36 weeks. She has a clear indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis given the positive GBS screen. Her reported reaction, hives and facial swelling (angioedema) to a penicillin-class antibiotic, is an IgE-mediated, high-risk allergy, so beta-lactams (including cephalosporins such as cefazolin) should be avoided.

With a high-risk penicillin allergy, agent selection depends on GBS susceptibility, which was not obtained here. In this high-risk-allergy patient with unknown susceptibility, the appropriate choice is IV vancomycin, weight-based dosing (20 mg/kg every 8 hours, with a maximum of 2 g per dose), which reliably covers GBS.

I would document the allergy, aim to administer the antibiotic at least 4 hours before delivery when feasible, and request clindamycin/erythromycin susceptibility testing on the isolate to inform any future care. prompt: A 3-year-old boy (14 kg) is admitted with acute gastroenteritis and moderate dehydration; he is now hemodynamically stable after an initial 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus and is tolerating small oral sips but still requires IV fluids overnight. prompt: A 58-year-old man with Child-Pugh B alcoholic cirrhosis (last drink 3 days ago) presents with two episodes of large-volume hematemesis and one melenic stool. He takes no beta-blocker. Vitals: HR 112, BP 92/58, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, afebrile. Exam: pale, mild ascites, no asterixis, alert and oriented.
